info.title: SAMM API
info.description:
SAMM public REST API — everything the admin portal does, scriptable.

## Authentication

Create a token in the admin portal (**System → API**, superadmin only) and send it
on every request:

```bash
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer samm_YOUR_TOKEN" https://your-samm/api/v1/me
```

The secret is shown **once** at creation; only its SHA-256 hash is stored. A token
carries **scopes** — per-resource grants such as `customers:read` / `customers:write`;
a `write` scope automatically includes the matching `read`. `GET /me` shows the
calling token's effective scopes. Revoking a token makes its calls fail immediately.

## Rate limits

Each token has its own per-minute limit (default 120, set at creation). Exceeding it
returns `429` with `Retry-After` and `X-RateLimit-Limit` / `X-RateLimit-Remaining`
headers — back off and retry.

## Conventions

* List endpoints accept `limit` / `offset` and return `{"total": n, "items": [...]}`.
* Errors: `401` missing/invalid/expired/revoked token · `403` token lacks the required
  scope · `404` not found · `409` duplicate · `422` validation error · `429` rate limit.
* All timestamps are ISO-8601 UTC; all byte counters are plain integers.

## Queued commands

Mutations that touch live accounting state (limit resets, card/group enable/disable,
validity extensions) are **not applied inside the request** — they are queued into the
audited command queue and applied by the `samm-radius` service within one tick
(a few seconds), exactly like the same clicks in the admin portal. These endpoints
reply `{"queued": true}`; poll `GET /commands` to watch your token's commands flip
to `applied`. Everything else (create/update/suspend/renew/pay …) is applied
immediately, and any needed router push (CoA) is queued automatically.

## Webhooks

Register an endpoint (`POST /webhooks` or the admin page) and pick events. Every
delivery carries `X-SAMM-Event` and `X-SAMM-Signature: sha256=<hex>` — the HMAC-SHA256
of the **raw body** with your endpoint's signing secret (returned once at creation):

```python
import hmac, hashlib

def verify(body: bytes, signature_header: str, secret: str) -> bool:
    calc = "sha256=" + hmac.new(secret.encode(), body, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
    return hmac.compare_digest(calc, signature_header)
```

`GET /webhooks/events` lists every event name and what it means — read it rather
than hard-coding the list, since subscribing to a name that does not exist creates
an endpoint that simply never fires. Among them, `alert.opened` / `alert.resolved`
carry the Alert Center's own transitions (router down, service down, rogue DHCP, a
new crash), already deduplicated by the alert engine, so a flapping link sends one
event rather than hundreds.

Failed deliveries retry with exponential backoff; an endpoint that keeps failing is
disabled automatically (re-enable with `POST /webhooks/{id}/enable`, or trial-run
with `POST /webhooks/{id}/test`).

## Two shapes of "expired"

A user is expired either because `status` says so, or because their
expiration limit is exhausted and they were **parked** on a next plan — still
authenticating, against a plan that gives them nothing. `GET /customers?status=expired`
and `/stats/overview` count both, exactly as the admin panel does. Filtering the
raw status field yourself will miss the second group, which is the group that has
already been cut off.

Server version: **5.1.15**

get.description:
List users with paging.

Filter by `status`, exact `username`, free-text `search`, `plan_id`,
`auto_renew`, and the expiry window (`expiring_before` / `expiring_after`).

The expiry filters and the `expiration_date` field exist because answering
"which users renew today" previously meant listing everyone and then
fetching each one individually — 675 extra requests against a production
box to build one work list. Scope: `customers:read`.

post.description: Create a user on a plan — applied immediately. Generates the initial subscription invoice unless `generate_invoice` is false; optionally pins the account to specific NAS via `allowed_nas_ids` (empty list = any NAS). Scope: `customers:write`.

get.description: Fetch one user by id. Scope: `customers:read`.

patch.description: Partially update profile fields, password, status, auto-renew or the NAS allow-list — omit a field to leave it unchanged. Emits a `customer.updated` webhook. Scope: `customers:write`.

delete.summary: Delete a user and all history
delete.description: Permanently delete the user and all their history (sessions, usage, invoices). Irreversible. Scope: `customers:write`.

post.description: Suspend the account; live sessions are dropped via CoA so access stops immediately. Scope: `customers:write`.
Reactivate a suspended account. Scope: `customers:write`.

Extend the expiration by one plan period, restore the original plan if the account was parked on an expired/throttle plan, and drop live sessions so the user re-authenticates with fresh attributes. Creates a renewal invoice when the plan has a price and `generate_invoice` is true (the new invoice id is in the response). Scope: `customers:write`.

post.summary: Reset one limit counter (queued, applied within one tick)
post.description: Queue a reset of one limit counter — `limitation_type` is quota | daily | uptime | expiration. Applied by samm-radius within one tick; track it via `GET /commands`. Scope: `customers:write`.
Change the user's plan (optionally generating an invoice). Live sessions receive the new speed via CoA. Scope: `customers:write`.
Queue a CoA Disconnect for every live session of this user. Scope: `coa:write`.

get.description: Usage snapshot: today's traffic, non-resettable lifetime totals, the per-limit resettable counters, and the most recent sessions. Scope: `customers:read`.

get.summary: Everything that happened to this user
get.description: The user's timeline: created, renewed, plan changes, suspensions, limit resets and every movement of money, newest first — the same rows the admin page shows, with the same amounts. Scope: `customers:read`.

post.description: Create a plan invoice for a user and plan; the amount defaults to the plan price and the entry is posted to the double-entry ledger. Scope: `billing:write`.

get.description: Full invoice detail: header, line items, recorded payments and the outstanding balance. Scope: `billing:read`.

delete.summary: Delete an invoice, closing it out correctly
delete.description:
Delete an invoice and leave the books consistent. Scope: `billing:write`.

Added because the API could create, pay and reopen an invoice but never
remove one — so an operator whose auto-renew sweep raised 675 invoices by
mistake had no way to undo it programmatically and had to be walked through
the panel.

This is NOT a raw delete. It routes through the accounting service, which:
  * voids the journal entries when nothing was ever collected,
  * writes the remainder off to Bad Debt when the invoice was part paid, so
    the cash and revenue already recognised are preserved,
  * skips the ledger entirely for an agent's off-ledger retail invoice.

Deleting the row without that leaves the receivable alive and attached to
nothing — money the company believes it is owed by no one.

get.description: Render the invoice as a downloadable PDF — the same renderer the portal and the Telegram bot use. Scope: `billing:read`.

post.description: Mark the invoice paid now and post the payment to the ledger. Emits an `invoice.paid` webhook on the next worker sweep. Scope: `billing:write`.
Reopen a paid invoice (reverses the payment posting). Scope: `billing:write`.

get.description: List live RADIUS sessions (no stop time yet), filterable by `username`. Scope: `sessions:read`.

post.description: Queue CoA Disconnect-Requests for all of the username's live sessions. Confirm delivery in `GET /coa-outbox`. Scope: `coa:write`.

post.summary: Push current plan speed to a user's live sessions (CoA-Update)
post.description: Queue a CoA-Update that pushes the user's current plan speed to their live sessions without disconnecting them. Scope: `coa:write`.

get.description: Inspect the CoA queue (pending / sent / NACK / done / failed) — useful to confirm a disconnect or speed change actually reached the router. Scope: `sessions:read`.

schema.description: pending | sent | nack | done | failed | obsolete | unconfigured | unreachable
schema.title: Status

parameters.description: pending | sent | nack | done | failed | obsolete | unconfigured | unreachable

post.description:
Put every failed CoA back on the queue with its attempt counter reset, so
`samm-radius` sends it again on the next tick.

Only rows that actually failed (`nack`, `failed`, `unreachable`,
`unconfigured`) are touched — a delivered CoA is never re-sent. Pass
`nas_id` after one router comes back rather than retrying the estate.
Scope: `coa:write`.

post.summary: Cancel every CoA still in flight
post.description:
Close every CoA still waiting to be delivered, as `obsolete`.

Obsolete, not failed: the operator decided these are no longer wanted, and
that must not read later as the router having refused them. Use it after a
change of plan, or when a backlog would push a stale rate to users
whose plan has since moved on. Scope: `coa:write`.

get.description: Inventory of RADIUS NAS and monitor-only MikroTiks, with reachability (last ping) and the identity/model/RouterOS metadata synced by samm-worker. Scope: `routers:read`.

get.summary: One router, with its health and its uplinks
get.description:
One router in full: the inventory row, its current health state and
open-finding count, and every interface SAMM has classified — which one is
the internet, what decided that, and whether an operator pinned it by hand.

"Which interface is the internet on" used to be answered three different
ways in three different places and stored nowhere. It is one answer now,
and this is where an integration reads it. Scope: `routers:read`.

get.summary: Interface throughput history for one router
get.description:
Interface throughput over a window, in bits per second — the same series the dashboard draws.

`win` is minutes and snaps to one of 10/30/60/180. `iface` limits it to a
single interface name; omitted, every interface on the router is summed.

The number of points is derived from how often this install actually polls,
never finer, so a bucket always contains at least one real sample. Ask for
10 minutes on a router polled every 30s and you get 20 points, not 40 with
every other one empty. Scope: `routers:read`.

get.summary: Read any RouterOS menu on a router (secrets masked)
get.description:
Everything `print` shows for that menu, as JSON, with passwords and keys
masked. Filters compare values exactly (yes/true and no/false are the same).
Scope: `routers:diagnose`.

One change on an allow-listed menu (see the module docs). The item is
read before and after; both go to the Admin Log with `reason`, masked.
Exactly one item is changed: a `match` that fits several is refused.
Scope: `routers:write`.

get.summary: Investigate one PPPoE user on a router
get.description:
One call for "connects but no internet" / "cannot connect": the router's
PPP AAA settings, any LOCAL secret with this name (which the router answers
itself, without asking SAMM), the live session and the address it got, the
profile it uses, that profile's pool, the NAT rules, and the log lines
mentioning the user. `findings` states what looks wrong in plain words.
Scope: `routers:diagnose`.

get.summary: A user's radio as the access points see it
get.description:
Signal (dBm and a quality word), SNR, Tx/Rx rate, CCQ and uptime of this
user's radio, read live from every MikroTik SAMM logs in to. Scope:
`routers:diagnose`.

get.summary: Ping, traceroute or DNS lookup FROM the router
get.description:
The same tools as the panel's Network Tools, run on the router itself:
"does this NAS reach the internet / SAMM / the upstream?". Scope:
`routers:diagnose`.

parameters.name: target

schema.description: Address or host name, e.g. 8.8.8.8 or google.com
schema.title: Target

parameters.description: Address or host name, e.g. 8.8.8.8 or google.com

get.summary: The router's RADIUS clients and their live counters
get.description:
Each /radius entry with `/radius monitor` counters (requests, accepts,
rejects, timeouts, bad replies) and /radius incoming. Rising timeouts mean
the router cannot reach SAMM; rising bad replies mean a secret mismatch.
Scope: `routers:diagnose`.

post.summary: Run a RouterOS script on a router and return its output
post.description:
Runs the script on the router (`:execute ... as-string`) and returns what
it printed. For anything the menus cannot express: PCC load balancing,
mangle, routing tables, several changes at once. A script that names
SAMM's link to the router (/user, /ip service, /radius, reset-configuration,
SAMM-AUTOSEC rules) is refused. Output is capped by RouterOS; keep long jobs
short or split them. Scope: `routers:write`.

get.summary: The health board: every router, worst first
get.description:
Every router SAMM watches, with its health state, score, open-finding
counts and the single worst reason — ordered worst first, exactly as the
Network Health board orders it.

`state` is the summary an alerting rule wants: `down` is unreachable,
`fault` is answering but broken (a critical finding on a live router),
`warn` is degraded, `ok` is clean, and null means it has not been checked
yet. Scope: `routers:read`.

parameters.name: state

schema.description: Only routers in this state: down | fault | warn | ok
schema.title: State

parameters.description: Only routers in this state: down | fault | warn | ok

get.description:
What is actually wrong, one row per problem, newest-worst first.

A finding keeps its `finding_key` for as long as the problem persists, so a
ticket raised against one can be closed when it stops coming back rather
than re-raised on every poll. `status=resolved` shows what cleared and
when. Scope: `routers:read`.

The map as data: every device SAMM has seen and every link between them.

A node with a null `nas_id` is a device discovered on the network that SAMM
does not manage — a user's own switch, an unregistered MikroTik, a
third-party box that answers neighbour discovery. Those are the interesting
ones: they are how an unauthorised device gets noticed.

Edges are stored once per link, not once per direction, even though both
ends usually report each other; `a_node_id` / `b_node_id` are ordered
canonically, so a link is stable to compare between polls. Scope:
`routers:read`.

parameters.name: include_hidden

schema.description: Include nodes an operator hid on the map
schema.title: Include Hidden

parameters.description: Include nodes an operator hid on the map

get.description:
Search the audit trail. Scope: `logs:read`.

Every filter is optional and they AND together, so "everything that touched
user 412 this week" is one call:

    /api/v1/audit?entity_type=user&entity_id=412&since=2026-08-01

`before`/`after` hold the changed fields and are omitted unless
`include_payload=true`, because they dominate the response and support
usually wants the shape of what happened first, then one row in detail.

get.summary: Who has been acting on this install
get.description:
Distinct actors with a count and their last action. Scope: `logs:read`.

Answers "who is touching this system" in one call — including API tokens,
which appear as `api:<token name>`.

Every authentication attempt and its verdict. Scope: `logs:read`.

`radacct` only records sessions that were ACCEPTED, so a user being
turned away leaves no trace there — they simply stop appearing. This reads
`radius.radpostauth`, which records the reply either way, so
"are they being rejected, or not even trying?" is answerable.

get.summary: Can this user authenticate, and if not, why
get.description:
One call that answers the support question. Scope: `customers:read`.

Checks, in the order that actually decides the outcome:

  * the subscriber exists and is not suspended
  * the expiry the PANEL shows (COALESCE(override, limit state))
  * the expiry the ENFORCEMENT ENGINE reads (limit state alone)
  * whether those two disagree — the failure that took a village offline:
    the screen said "active, 2 days left" while the sweep re-expired them
    every cycle and RADIUS refused every reconnect
  * any exhausted limit
  * the most recent authentication verdict

`blocked` is the verdict; `reasons` says why in plain words.

post.summary: Set expiry and/or status on many users
post.description:
Apply one change to many users. Scope: `customers:write`.

Returns a result per user — `ok`, `skipped` with a reason, or
`error` — because a bulk call that answers only "437 done" is unusable when
the question is "which ones did not, and why".

Setting `expiration_date` writes BOTH the admin override and the limit
state the expiration sweep reads. Writing only one is what let a screen
show "active" while RADIUS refused every reconnect.

get.description: List card groups with per-status card counts. Scope: `cards:read`.

post.summary: Create a card group and generate its cards
post.description: Create a voucher group and generate `count` cards in it. The group defines the speed and optional quota / uptime / expiration limits shared by all of its cards; username/password recipes control how card credentials are generated. Returns 403 when the licensed card cap would be exceeded. Scope: `cards:write`.

get.description: List a group's cards (username, password, status), filterable by `status` (unused | active | exhausted | disabled). Scope: `cards:read`.

post.summary: Add cards to an existing group
post.description: Generate `count` additional cards using the group's existing username/password recipe. Scope: `cards:write`.

get.description: Group configuration plus card counts by status. Scope: `cards:read`.

post.summary: Enable a group (queued, applied within one tick)
post.description: Queue enabling of the whole group (applied by samm-radius within one tick; track via `GET /commands`). Scope: `cards:write`.

post.summary: Disable a group and drop its live sessions (queued)
post.description: Queue disabling of the whole group; live card sessions are dropped when it applies. Scope: `cards:write`.
Queue a new `valid_until` date for the group — must be later than the current one. Scope: `cards:write`.

get.description: Printable voucher sheet (PDF) for the group, with the ISP name/logo from Settings; pass `only_unused=true` to print unsold cards only. Scope: `cards:read`.
One card with its per-limit counters and lifetime usage totals. Scope: `cards:read`.

post.summary: Enable a card (queued, applied within one tick)
post.description: Queue re-enabling of a single card. Scope: `cards:write`.

post.summary: Disable a card and drop its live session (queued)
post.description: Queue disabling of a single card; its live session is dropped when it applies. Scope: `cards:write`.
Queue a reset of one card limit counter — `kind` is quota | uptime | expiration. Scope: `cards:write`.

get.summary: List guest passcodes that were handed out
get.description:
The guest register, newest first: who signed themselves up, the passcode
they were given, how it was sent and whether it arrived. Scope: `guests:read`.

Several jurisdictions require an ISP to be able to say who used a guest
network — this is that record, and rows are kept until an admin deletes one.

`contact` matches the way the one-live-code rule does: on the CANONICAL
contact, so a mobile must be given in E.164 (`+961…`). Names are not
searchable here — people share names, and contact alone is the identity the
feature keys on.

schema.description: true = passcode still usable; false = expired or voided

parameters.description: true = passcode still usable; false = expired or voided

schema.description: Exact mobile (E.164, e.g. +96181507933) or email, case-insensitive
schema.title: Contact

parameters.description: Exact mobile (E.164, e.g. +96181507933) or email, case-insensitive

get.summary: Self Service license position and register counters
get.description:
Where this install stands on Self Service: the master switch, the
licensed passcodes-per-day and how much of today is spent, the add-on tier
with its own expiry, and the register's counters. Scope: `guests:read`.

`allowance` and `remaining` are **null** when the rate is unlimited
(Self Service Max) — the -1 sentinel samm.settings uses never leaves SAMM.

Read from the SQL side (`samm.guest_daily_allowance()` and the same two-term
count) rather than from the license token, exactly as the admin Self Service
page is: the number a guest actually meets is the one the RADIUS gate
computes, and a second opinion here could disagree with the refusal on their
screen. `used` therefore counts billable handouts since the install's own day
started PLUS registrations still in flight — a slot is claimed when it is
promised, not when the passcode is minted.
List endpoints including delivery health: consecutive fail streak, last successful delivery and last error. Scope: `webhooks:manage`.

post.description: Register an endpoint. The HMAC signing secret is returned ONCE in this response — store it; deliveries are signed with it (`X-SAMM-Signature`). Unknown event names are ignored; at least one valid event is required. Scope: `webhooks:manage`.

get.summary: Every event an endpoint can subscribe to
get.description:
The event catalogue, with what each one means.

Subscribing to a name that does not exist is silently useless — the endpoint
is created and simply never fires — so a client that builds its own
subscription list needs to read the catalogue rather than guess it. The
names here are the only values `POST /webhooks` accepts.

delete.description: Delete the endpoint and its queued deliveries. Scope: `webhooks:manage`.

post.description: Re-enable a disabled endpoint and reset its fail streak. Scope: `webhooks:manage`.
Stop deliveries to this endpoint (kept configured, reversible). Scope: `webhooks:manage`.

post.summary: Queue a test event to this endpoint
post.description: Queue a `webhook.test` event, delivered on the next samm-worker tick — verify your receiver and signature check end-to-end. Scope: `webhooks:manage`.

get.description: The export `kind`s available at `/accounting/export/{kind}`. Scope: `accounting:read`.

Export one set of books. `kind` ∈ journal, chart_of_accounts, invoices,
trial_balance, pnl, balance_sheet. `format=csv` streams a download; default
JSON returns `{kind, columns, rows}`. Voided journal entries are excluded, so
an export always reconciles with the admin reports. Scope: `accounting:read`.

parameters.name: as_of

schema.description: YYYY-MM-DD for point-in-time exports (trial_balance, balance_sheet, chart_of_accounts)
schema.title: As Of

parameters.description: YYYY-MM-DD for point-in-time exports (trial_balance, balance_sheet, chart_of_accounts)

get.summary: Full health + collection snapshot for support
get.description: One-shot health snapshot: service liveness, data-collection freshness, per-router sync ages, recent self-heal events and license state. Scope: `diagnostics:read`.

Incidents from samm.error_report, newest first — deduplicated by
fingerprint with an occurrence count, so a crash loop is ONE row saying
"×4,000" rather than four thousand rows. The traceback is omitted here (it is
long and this is the triage list); fetch one incident for it.

`reported` tells you whether the operator already flagged it for upload, and
`sent` whether it reached SecuryTik — useful when a user says "I sent
you the error" and nothing arrived. Scope: `errors:read`.

get.summary: Admin alerts raised on this install
get.description:
The Alert Center's own view, read-only, from off the box.

/diagnostics answers "is the machine healthy"; this answers the question
that follows it — "and has the install been TELLING anyone it isn't". They
are not the same: an alert can be open for two days with a healthy snapshot
right now, and a bell nobody has clicked is the most common reason a
user says nothing warned them.

Default is everything unresolved (pending + open + acknowledged), newest
first, because that is the triage question. Pass `status=resolved` for what
cleared. Rides `diagnostics:read`: subjects name a router or a service, not
a user, so this is health data — nothing here needs the separate
consent that tracebacks and daemon logs do.

parameters.name: status

schema.description: pending | open | acknowledged | resolved. Omit for everything still live.
schema.title: Status

parameters.description: pending | open | acknowledged | resolved. Omit for everything still live.

get.description:
One incident by numeric id, incident_id or fingerprint — whichever the
user quoted. Includes the full traceback and captured context, both
text-masked. Scope: `errors:read`.

The live samm.settings tunables that explain most misbehaviour, plus the
schema level. An allow-list — credentials and gateway keys are never in it,
and any value whose key still looks like a secret is masked anyway.

`schema_version` is the highest applied migration, which is the first thing
to check when an install behaves like an older release. Scope:
`diagnostics:read`.

Runs the checks a support engineer would run by hand and returns a
pass/fail per check with a one-line reason.

Unlike /diagnostics — which reports what the install has RECORDED — these
probe the current state: the database answers, the daemons have beaten
recently, every router has been reached, the disk has room, and the AAA
tables are reachable. `ok` is the summary: false means at least one check
failed. Scope: `diagnostics:read`.

get.summary: Can this install reach what SAMM depends on?
get.description:
Reachability of every service SAMM talks to, from the install's network.

Read-only, and deliberately not a URL fetcher: the targets are the fixed
list above. `ok` means the host ANSWERED — an HTTP 403/405 to a HEAD still
proves the path is open, so read `status` for what it said and `error` for
why nothing came back. `blocked` is the short answer.

All targets are probed in parallel behind one deadline, because the whole
point is that a blocked host does not fail fast: a DNS-black-holed name
stalls per resolved address, so probing seven of them in sequence could
outlast the request itself. Scope: `diagnostics:read`.

get.summary: Capped, redacted tail of a SAMM unit or log file
get.description:
A bounded tail of one SAMM unit, newest last, with secret shapes masked.

Deliberately narrow: a fixed unit allow-list, at most 1000 lines, at most a
day back. Daemon output can quote usernames and addresses, which is why this
has its own scope instead of riding on `diagnostics:read` — a user grants
log access as a separate, conscious decision. Scope: `logs:read`.

`file=radius.log` reads FreeRADIUS's own log instead of the journal, and it
is not a convenience. FreeRADIUS logs to `${logdir}/radius.log`, so its
startup failures never reach journald: the journal shows only the
`ExecStartPre` config check saying "Configuration appears to be OK" followed
by a bare `status=1/FAILURE`. Two user outages were diagnosable ONLY
from this file, and reaching it meant asking the operator for shell access.
Reach for it whenever freeradius will not start.

get.summary: Host + unit facts support used to ask for by SSH
get.description:
The `systemctl show` / `ls -ld` / `--version` answers, over the API.

Every field here was something support had to obtain by asking the operator
for a shell session during the 2026-08 outages. The unit facts in particular
decide the diagnosis outright: a freeradius unit with an EMPTY
`RuntimeDirectory` cannot recreate /run/freeradius after a reboot, which is
what took two ISPs offline — and it is invisible from every other endpoint.
Read-only, no shell, no secrets. Scope: `diagnostics:read`.

get.summary: Per-service state for every unit SAMM needs
get.description:
What is running, what is enabled at boot, and how often it has restarted.

/diagnostics reports the four daemons that stamp a heartbeat. This reports
every unit the install actually depends on — including freeradius, nginx and
postgresql, none of which heartbeat, and one of which takes the whole ISP
offline when it dies. Read-only. Scope: `diagnostics:read`.

post.description:
Restart a single SAMM-owned unit.

The one endpoint in this router that changes the machine, which is why it
needs `services:write` — a scope no support token carries by default. During
the 2026-08 outages the only way to restart a user's FreeRADIUS was to
ask them for a shell; this closes that, without letting a read-only token do
it by accident.

Allow-listed against SAMM's own catalogue: never an arbitrary unit name,
which would make this a systemctl proxy for the whole box. `samm-api` is
handed to the oneshot restart unit because a process cannot restart itself
inside the request that asked for it.

get.description:
Why messages are not arriving — the question behind most support mail.

Three things, in one call: how each channel is configured (values through
`_redact()`, so the SMTP password and the WhatsApp access token never leave
the box), what the queue has done in the last 24 h per channel and status,
and the errors themselves. `samm.notif_outbox.last_error` is where a
rejected SMTP login, an expired Meta token or an unlinked WhatsApp number
actually says so, and nothing outside this endpoint could read it.

For the unofficial QR bridge specifically, pair this with
`GET /support/logs?unit=samm-wa-bridge`. Scope: `diagnostics:read`.

get.summary: Backlog and failures in every SAMM queue
get.description:
The three queues that make an install look broken while it is healthy.

A CoA backlog means speed and disconnect changes are not reaching the
routers, so an operator sees "the plan change did nothing". Unapplied
`audit_log` rows mean samm-radius is not draining, so panel actions appear
to be ignored. A webhook backlog means the customer's own integration is
down, not SAMM. Each one is a different owner, and they are indistinguishable
from the panel. (`notif_outbox` has its own endpoint, /support/notifications.)

Same per-status indexed ranges as there, for the same reason. Scope:
`diagnostics:read`.

get.summary: Licence state, and what it is sized against
get.description:
Where an install stands with the licence authority, and why.

`license_last_error` is the whole answer to "it says unlicensed" — a DNS
block on license-samm.securytik.com, a clock so far out that the token
fails validation, a device id that was re-linked elsewhere. The counts are
what the licence is measured against, so an over-limit install shows up
here rather than in a support round trip.

Every `license_*` setting is included EXCEPT the tokens: `_redact()` masks
any key that looks like a credential, which covers `license_token` and
`license_device_token`. Scope: `diagnostics:read`.

get.summary: Update state, and why the last one did not land
get.description:
What this install knows about updates, and how its schema compares.

An update that fails leaves `update_apply_error` and a stalled
`update_apply_phase` behind, and until now neither was readable remotely —
nor was the updater's journal, which is the other half (now
`GET /support/logs?unit=samm-updater`).

`schema_head` against `SAMM_VERSION` is the second question support asks:
an install running new code on an old schema behaves like neither release.
Scope: `diagnostics:read`.

get.summary: PostgreSQL health and the connection pool
get.description:
The pool, the server, and what is holding either of them.

This exists because of one incident shape that reaches us repeatedly: the
panel starts timing out and the captured traceback says
`QueuePool limit of size N overflow M reached` — SQLAlchemy could not get a
connection. That single line cannot distinguish a leak in SAMM from a
Postgres that is refusing connections from a long query holding a lock, and
the difference decides the fix. All three are here.

`pg_stat_activity` shows the query text of OUR OWN backends only (SAMM
connects as one unprivileged role), which is the set that matters; other
roles appear as a state with no text. Query text is masked anyway. Scope:
`diagnostics:read`.

get.summary: Are backups running, and did the last one work?
get.description:
The nightly backup's own record, plus what is actually on disk.

A scheduled backup that has been failing silently is only discovered when
someone needs it. `_backup_auto_last_error` is written every time the sweep
fails and read by nobody; this puts it where support can see it without a
shell, next to the files it claims to have written.

Since SAMM has no update rollback, a current backup is the only floor under
a bad update — so "is this install backed up" is a release question, not
just a support one. Scope: `diagnostics:read`.

get.summary: Admin accounts and how many users each owns
get.description:
List admins with their assigned-subscriber counts. Scope: `customers:read`.

Feed `id` to `GET /customers?assigned_admin_id=` (or pass the username to
`?assigned_admin=`). `customer_count` is the number that lets an operator
confirm they picked the right person before acting on them — "Ali, the one
with 456" is checkable in a way a bare id is not.

`orphaned_customers` counts users whose `assigned_admin_id` points at
an admin row that no longer exists. samm.user.assigned_admin_id carries no
foreign key, so deleting an admin silently strands their users; they
appear under no admin at all and are invisible to every per-admin filter.

Mutations like resets and card/group status changes are queued into the
audit-log command queue and applied by samm-radius within one tick. This
endpoint reports only the calling token's own commands.
